Predicted in the 1970s by NASA physicist Donald Kessler, this chain of orbital smashups could make the space around Earth unusable and unsafe. The dangerous tipping might be nearer than some think. Humankind's utilization of space is at an inflection point, as companies such as SpaceX , Blue Origin and Amazon plan to launch constellations of hundreds of thousands of telecommunication satellites and orbiting data centers in the coming years. " Low Earth orbit looks like lots of other resources that we have trashed as economic actors," Daniel Kaffine, a professor of environmental and resource economics at University of Colorado Boulder, told Space.com. "Waiting until it gets really, really bad to start implementing any of these types of policy interventions has historically been what we have done," Kaffine added. "But maybe we can think about things we can do right now." SpaceX has been relatively quiet about Starfall, which debuted this past June on a Falcon 9 launch from the Cape. The payloads of SpaceX's Bandwagon-5 rideshare mission, seen in a prelaunch photo. (Image credit: SpaceX) That June 23 flight was a dedicated demonstration mission for Starfall, designed to show that the capsule can fly in a controlled fashion and survive the harrowing downward trip through Earth's atmosphere . Indeed, most of the details that we have about the capsule come from an environmental assessment that was published by the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration in May. candidates.title: Starwatch: Orionid meteor shower to peak on night skies
candidates.raw_excerpt:
The annual Orionid meteor shower is set to peak on the night of October 21 to 22, offering stargazers a chance to witness one of the major meteor showers of the year. Around 20 meteors can be seen per hour under ideal viewing conditions.

The Orionids are active each year from October 2 to November 7. With a rate of about 10 to 20 meteors per hour, they are considered to be one of the most beautiful showers of the year, according to NASA.

The meteor shower is created by dust and debris left behind by Comet 1P/Halley. As Earth travels along its orbit around the sun, it passes through particles shed by the comet during its journeys through the inner solar system. These tiny particles collide with Earth's atmosphere at extremely high speeds, producing the bright streaks of light known as meteors.

As Earth crosses different parts of this debris stream twice each year, the dust grains become two annual meteor showers – the Orionids in October and the Eta Aquariids in May.

Japan launched an uncrewed spacecraft toward the Martian moon Phobos on Tuesday on a mission intended to become the first to collect samples from the small, rocky body and return them to Earth for analysis.

The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's (JAXA) Martian Moons eXploration spacecraft lifted off aboard an H3 rocket before dawn from the Tanegashima Space Center in southwestern Japan.

The spacecraft is expected to reach Mars in August 2027 and return the samples to Earth in 2031. JAXA hopes the mission will shed light on the origin of the two Martian moons and deepen our understanding of the solar system's early stages.

Phobos, the larger of the two moons, orbits Mars three times a day. It has an irregular shape with dimensions of about 27 km by 22 km by 18 km, and it orbits roughly 6,000 km above the Martian surface.

JAXA aims to collect at least 10 grams of material from the surface to return to Earth for analysis.

The launch marked the first interplanetary mission for Japan's H3 rocket. The country's flagship launcher experienced a high-profile failure on its inaugural flight in 2023 when its second-stage engine failed to ignite, but it has since completed a series of mostly successful launches.

candidates.title: JAXA’s MMX Enroute to Mars To Return Samples of Phobos
candidates.raw_excerpt: The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency successfully launch the Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission this afternoon EDT. MMX will not land on Mars, but instead explore its two moons, Phobos and Deimos, returning samples of Phobos to Earth in 2031. Japan and the U.S. have returned samples of asteroids, but this will be the first from a moon other than our own and could solve the mystery of whether Phobos is an asteroid captured by Mars’s gravity or a piece of Mars ejected by a collision. MMX lifted off on a Mitsubishi Heavy Industries H3 rocket at 3:41 pm EDT today, Monday, October 19, 2026 — the early hours (4:41 am) of Tuesday, October 20, at the Tanegashima launch site. Liftoff of JAXA’s Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) spacecraft from Tanegashima, Japan, October 19, 2026 EDT (October 20 local time in Japan). Screenshot from JAXA webcast . MMX is headed to Mars, but instead of landing it will enter a Quasi-Satellite Orbit or QSO. That will enable it study the moons Phobos and Deimos including a landing on Phobos to collect samples for return to Earth. The two small moons are a scientific mystery. The larger of the two, Phobos, is just 22 kilometers (14 miles) in diameter. Deimos is even smaller, 12 km (7.5 mi). Are they asteroids captured by the gravity of Mars, or ejecta from a collision between Mars and another celestial object eons ago? The asteroid belt with its millions of asteroids — rocks left over from the formation of the solar system — lies between Mars and Jupiter. But the orbits of Phobos and Deimos are circular and aligned with Mars’s equator, not tilted. That suggests to others they weren’t randomly pulled into orbit around Mars, but instead that an impact on Mars might have ejected material into orbit where it collected into these moons. NASA rendering of Phobos and Deimos orbiting Mars. Credit: NASA Today’s launch was just the first leg of the journey, which will last five years. MMX will arrive at Mars in August 2027 and descend to land on Phobos

(Image credit: contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data (2026), processed by ESA) Antarctica is a magnificent sight, and that beauty is visible all the way from space. What is it? Orbiting planet Earth, the European Space Agency's (ESA) Copernicus Sentinel-3 mission captured a close-up of West Antarctica. Winter is ending in the Southern Hemisphere, meaning this is the peak of icy weather and sea ice in the Arctic. In this image snapped by Sentinel-3, you can see a massive swath of ice which includes Elephant Island on the left-hand side. An ice-covered island off the Antarctic coast, Elephant Island floats in the Southern Ocean. It got its name both from the island's shape, which some liken to that of an elephant's head, and the fact that the island is home to a community of elephant seals. Why is it incredible? While a seal-inhabited island on the left floats near the Antarctic coast, across the water is a vast, frozen landscape. In just this snapshot, you can see about between 746 and 1,056 miles (1,200 to 1,700 kilometers) of the icy continent. This image was captured on Sept. 30, 2026. In the Southern Hemisphere, that was just past the end of winter. The absolute peak for sea ice in Antarctica fell just a couple weeks before, on Sept. 14, according to the National Snow and Ice Data Center, ESA reported . So in this one snapshot, we can see a near-maximum for sea ice in the Antarctic, spanning hundreds of miles. In observing our own planet from space, we are able to peer across vast landscapes, capturing important observational data. This is especially critical for the Antarctic as, with the progression of climate change , this sea ice continues to dwindle , adding to sea level rise among other serious consequences across the planet.

Among the many questions we have about Earth's lone natural satellite, one remains preeminent: what are the moon's origins , and how long has it orbited Earth? Today, the leading theory among astronomers is that deep in our planet's past — perhaps within roughly the first 100 million years of solar system history — Earth collided with a planet-sized object, creating the moon within a period that may have been as short as just a few hours . Known as the giant-impact hypothesis, this proposed event involves a hypothetical Mars-sized protoplanet astronomers call Theia. The material ejected into orbit by the powerful impact in question would have accumulated afterward, forming the moon that we observe today. What do we know? Birth of a lunar origin hypothesis The evolution of this striking solution to one of the moon's most enduring mysteries goes back to 1946, when geologist Reginald Aldworth Daly was among the first to suggest that an impact event might explain the formation of the moon. Before Daly, scientists had been leaning toward theories that involved Earth's rapid spin billions of years ago, when each day may have at one time lasted as little as 2 or 3 hours . Decades later in the 1970s, researchers William Hartmann and Donald Davis developed their own models involving collisions of large bodies left over from planetary formation, which could collide with younger planets. Building on such ideas, other researchers went on to propose similar scenarios between the early Earth and a Mars-sized object. The 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17) opened on Sunday in Yerevan, the capital of Armenia, with countries set to conduct the first global review of collective progress in implementing the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF).

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan declared the conference open, calling for countries to translate their commitments into concrete actions and measurable results as the 2030 deadline for the framework's targets approaches.

Astrid Schomaker, executive secretary of the Convention on Biological Diversity, expressed hope that COP17 would demonstrate the multilateralism works and that the international community can fulfill its commitments.

She said the assessment of the KMGBF and countries' national reports would help identify implementation gaps and guide efforts to address them.

Adopted in 2022, the KMGBF aims to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030, with a vision of living in harmony with nature by 2050. The global review will assess progress, identify gaps and help determine priority actions to accelerate implementation.

COP17 will run from October 19 to 30 under the theme "Taking Action for Nature."
